action_criteria.rationale: The outside CT reported enlarged ventricles only; MRI must measure the markers and exclude an obstructing lesion before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, electrolytes, renal function, TSH and vitamin B12; RPR and HIV non-reactive
action_criteria.label: Targeted labs for reversible contributors
action_criteria.rationale: With a thiazide and no other metabolic clue, an electrolyte, thyroid and B12 screen is good practice but does not decide iNPH.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 16 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; 38 mL removed; TUG 24 to 16 s (33%) at 24 hours
action_criteria.label: CSF tap test: opening pressure, routine CSF and removal of 30-50 mL
action_criteria.rationale: Removing 38 mL with normal opening pressure and normal CSF content tests whether his gait improves when CSF is drained.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 18 s at 2 hours and 16 s at 24 hours (33% faster), 10-m walk 12 s (33% faster), MoCA 26/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating his TUG and 10-m walk at 2 and 24 hours after the 38 mL tap shows whether his gait responds to CSF removal.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the cognitive decline to obstructive sleep apnoea in a CPAP-adherent patient with ventriculomegaly, DESH and an objective tap response
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning in a patient with ventriculomegaly, DESH and an objective tap response
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 33% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Continue CPAP; untreated OSA contributes to cognitive slowing
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: He has had no seizures or fluctuating awareness, so an EEG does not address his progressive gait and cognitive syndrome.
His falls happened while walking or turning without loss of consciousness, so an ECG does not explain them.
He has no cardiac symptoms or embolic events, and an echocardiogram does not inform the iNPH work-up.
An outside CT already showed enlarged ventricles; MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, DESH and hippocampi better.
There is no syncope or palpitation history, so ambulatory rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
A two-year course without rapid decline, fever or inflammatory features gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 1 white matter change without lacunes is too mild to explain his gait and cognition, which improve after CSF removal.
No tremor or rigidity, full eye movements and a wide-based gait that improves after the tap argue against parkinsonism.
Gait came first, recall improves with cueing, MTA is 1 and the MoCA rises after the tap, which fit a frontal-subcortical rather than an amnestic profile.

differential.diagnosis: Cognitive impairment related to obstructive sleep apnoea
differential.key_features: He is CPAP-adherent, and OSA does not produce ventriculomegaly, a magnetic gait or urge incontinence.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles disproportionate to cortical volume loss, tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle argue against ex-vacuo enlargement.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic) communicating hydrocephalus
differential.key_features: There is no history of head injury, haemorrhage or meningitis before the gait decline.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires an insidious gait disturbance after age 40, progressing over at least 3 to 6 months without an antecedent cause, plus cognitive or urinary symptoms; he has all three over two years [Relkin_2005]
MRI shows Evans index 0.36 with both DESH components, a callosal angle of 78 degrees and temporal horn enlargement, with no obstructing lesion [Relkin_2005]
Opening pressure 16 cmH2O with normal CSF content meets the pressure criterion [Relkin_2005]

After removal of 38 mL, TUG fell from 24 to 16 s (33%) at 24 hours and the 10-m walk from 18 to 12 s; an improvement of 10% or more in TUG is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off
The tap test has a sensitivity of 26% to 61% and a PPV of 73% to 100%, so a clear response supports shunting while a negative tap would not have excluded it [Marmarou_2005]
Treated OSA does not explain a magnetic gait, urge incontinence or ventriculomegaly with DESH

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: He is CPAP-adherent, and OSA does not cause ventriculomegaly, DESH, a magnetic gait or urge incontinence.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Cognitive slowing is attributed to OSA-related cognitive impairment alone

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: iNPH in a 69-year-old retired principal: gait, urinary and cognitive symptoms, DESH on MRI and a clear tap response; OSA on CPAP as the cognitive red herring.
metadata.revision_reason: case-level re-audit of all NPH reviewer requests: the tap report is routed to CSF, timed gait/cognitive assessment is the required pre/post measure, the standalone neuropsychological battery and advanced imaging are removed from gold actions and callable authored follow-ups, laboratories remain optional, unrelated CSF assays are no longer returned for free, and the unsupported universal 20% response threshold is corrected

patient.chief_complaint: Slowly progressive gait problems, daytime incontinence, and difficulty remembering recent events; admitted for evaluation

patient.history_present_illness: A 69-year-old retired high school principal with hypertension and well-controlled obstructive sleep apnea (CPAP-compliant) was admitted following referral from his primary care physician for a two-year history of progressive gait difficulty, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline. He first noticed gait problems two years ago while trying to walk quickly to catch a bus; he found he could not move his legs fast enough and had to abandon the attempt. Over the subsequent months his walking progressively slowed and he began to take shorter steps. His wife noticed a 'magnetic quality' to his gait. He has had three falls, two in the kitchen and one on a garden path, all while walking or turning and none causing significant injury or loss of consciousness. He now avoids uneven surfaces and has limited his walking to short distances inside the house. Urinary incontinence began approximately 18 months ago. He describes strong urgency and insufficient time to reach the bathroom, resulting in accidents approximately twice per week. He initially attributed this to rushing and drinking too much coffee, but reducing his fluid intake had no effect. His wife notes he repeats himself in conversation, frequently cannot recall what was said 5 minutes prior, and has difficulty planning a dinner party they used to host effortlessly. A cognitive assessment ordered by his primary care physician 4 months ago was reported as showing executive dysfunction and slowed processing speed. A head CT obtained at that time at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, fully oriented. Slowed responses, no aphasia. Good insight into his deficits. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
